sources.title: Tackling Climate Change, Land Degradation and Fragility: Diagnosing Drivers of Climate and Environmental Fragility in Burundi’s Colline Landscapes: Towards a Multi-Sector Investment Plan to Scale up Climate Resilience
sources.organization: World Bank and Government of Burundi
sources.temporal_coverage: Historical climate series, mid-century projections, and spatial multi-risk assessment reported in 2022
sources.methodology: Combines climate projections, land-degradation modeling and spatial multi-risk analysis of 2,616 collines.
sources.limitations: Risk scores combine hazards, exposure, vulnerability, coping capacity and past conflict; they are not causal estimates. Rainfall projections vary.

sources.title: Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC) / Burundi
sources.temporal_coverage: National vulnerability assessment and climate projections through 2050, as reported in 2015
sources.methodology: Summarizes prior national communications, an ACCES soil-and-water vulnerability analysis, and general circulation model projections.
sources.limitations: 2015 assessment using earlier studies; the cited projection passage does not name a scenario. Adaptation measures describe plans, not evaluated results.

claims.locator: PDF p. 8, climate outlook summary
claims.paraphrase: The report projects 0.5–1.0°C warming for 2040–2060 versus 1981–2000, with uncertain north–south rainfall differences.
claims.scenario: The inspected summary does not specify it.
claims.limitations: Regional precipitation direction varies across models; the report notes projection uncertainty.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 50–51, colline multi-risk assessment and scoring note
claims.paraphrase: The composite assessment scores 347 of 2,616 collines at very high combined climate, environmental and fragility risk, and none at low or very low risk.
claims.limitations: A composite model result, not a count of observed climate impacts or evidence that climate caused fragility.

claims.locator: PDF p. 9, executive summary on fragility and land scarcity
claims.paraphrase: The report describes land scarcity as an existing source of intercommunal conflict and warns climate and land degradation may reduce arable productivity and intensify this pressure.
claims.scenario: The inspected summary does not specify it.
claims.limitations: The source presents a prospective risk pathway, not a causal evaluation or quantified forecast of conflict.

claims.locator: PDF p. 3, section 2.1, climate change impacts and vulnerability
claims.paraphrase: Prior national analysis projected 1–3°C higher annual mean temperature and roughly 10% more rainfall by 2050, with a disrupted seasonal regime.
claims.scenario: The inspected summary does not specify it.
claims.limitations: The INDC reports projections from prior national communication studies; its cited passage does not identify the emissions scenario.

claims.locator: PDF p. 3, section 2.1, ACCES vulnerability analysis
claims.paraphrase: The INDC identifies northern and northwestern vulnerability hotspots and flags the slope toward the Imbo Plain, northern terrain and central plateau as erosion-prone.
claims.limitations: The INDC cites an earlier integrated vulnerability analysis and does not give a date or quantitative score for these locations.

claims.locator: PDF p. 3, section 2.1 and Table 1, climate-related risks by sector
claims.paraphrase: The INDC lists groundwater shortage, lowland flooding, soil-fertility loss, crop-season changes and unpredictable pest movements among projected risks.
claims.scenario: The inspected summary does not specify it.
claims.limitations: These are risks stated in a 2015 national contribution drawing on older assessments, not observed outcomes attributable to climate change.

sources.title: Analysis of the Frequency and Impacts of Flooding in Chad
sources.organization: World Bank Sahel Adaptive Social Protection Program Technical Paper Series; Pierre E. Biscaye (external contributor)
sources.temporal_coverage: Flood incidence analysis over approximately 2012–2024 and modeled present-day exposure under 2020 conditions
sources.methodology: External technical study compares flood-hazard models, survey reports and satellite-detected floods, then maps population exposure using administrative and population datasets.
sources.limitations: Modeled exposure is not observed damage; estimates vary by flood model and population data. Some satellite years are missing and built-up areas can be harder to detect.

sources.title: Chad Economic Update: Improving Resilience to Floods

sources.methodology: Economic update combining flood-risk context, service data and climate-impact modeling summarized from the Sahel CCDR.
sources.limitations: The report relies partly on cited data; conflict and displacement statements do not evaluate specific flood events causally.

claims.locator: PDF p. 21, section 2.1.2; Table 1 and Figure 4 use 2020-condition estimates
claims.paraphrase: One model estimates over 4.2 million people, including 538,000 in N’Djamena, face at least 10 cm inundation in a 100-year flood.
claims.limitations: This is modeled exposure under 2020 conditions, not a count of people actually harmed; other models produce different estimates.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 13 and 19, section on differentiated flood vulnerability
claims.paraphrase: Rural vulnerability is tied to rain-fed farming and less durable homes; recent urban arrivals often settle in low-lying areas with weak drainage.
geographies: urban areas near lakes and rivers
claims.limitations: The report synthesizes cited studies and does not quantify the separate contribution of each vulnerability factor.

claims.locator: PDF p. 1, summary; section 3 on flood incidence
claims.paraphrase: The study identifies 2012, 2022 and 2024 among Chad’s notably damaging flood years.
claims.limitations: The report draws on multiple datasets whose observation periods and event definitions differ.

claims.locator: PDF p. 32, section 2, ‘Context and evolving disaster risk profile’
claims.paraphrase: The update reports slightly more drought events in 2002–2022 than in 1981–2001, with each event affecting 14.5% of the population on average.
claims.limitations: These are report-referenced event estimates; the cited comparison does not itself attribute the observed drought sequence to climate change.

claims.locator: PDF p. 32, section 2, service-access and coping-capacity discussion

claims.locator: PDF p. 13, executive summary on recent floods and displacement

claims.limitations: This is a broad report-level statement, not event-specific causal evidence or a measured conflict effect.

sources.title: Rwanda's 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0)
sources.temporal_coverage: Historical climate/disaster information and projections through 2050 reported in 2025
sources.methodology: NDC compiles national climate records, cited studies and adaptation priorities.
sources.limitations: Cited disaster estimates do not establish climate effects on conflict.

sources.title: Country Climate and Development Report: Rwanda - Technical Appendix
sources.temporal_coverage: Modeled crop and macroeconomic impacts under climate scenarios through 2050 and 2100
sources.methodology: Technical appendix uses Rwanda-specific crop, labor, health and flood damage functions in a computable general-equilibrium model.
sources.limitations: Scenario-dependent model using CMIP5 projections and a 2017 social accounting matrix; results are not observed impacts.

claims.locator: PDF p. 31, section 2.1, observed temperature and rainfall changes
claims.paraphrase: NDC reports about 1.4°C warming since 1970; rainy seasons shortened and intensified, especially in north and west.
claims.limitations: NDC cites national sources; regions differ.

claims.locator: PDF p. 32, projected national temperature change
claims.paraphrase: By around 2050, mean annual temperature is projected 1.5-2.5 degrees C above recent levels under RCP4.5/RCP8.5.
claims.limitations: Scenario projection, not deterministic.

claims.locator: PDF p. 115, Box 1, May 2023 flood and landslide impacts
claims.paraphrase: Heavy rain triggered May 2023 floods and landslides, causing 131 deaths and over 110 injuries along the Nile-Congo divide.
claims.limitations: NDC cites government counts; event attribution is not stated.

claims.locator: PDF p. 115, 2024 East Africa rainfall attribution summary
claims.paraphrase: A cited study says 2024 East African rains/floods were twice as likely and 5% more intense due to human climate influence.
claims.limitations: Regional attribution estimate, not Rwanda-only.

claims.locator: PDF p. 116, housing damage and temporary accommodation from extreme events
claims.paraphrase: NDC reports 58,760 homes damaged/destroyed by extreme weather in 2016-24; 18,000 people moved to temporary shelter in 2023.
claims.limitations: Aggregate figures; no hazard breakdown.

claims.locator: PDF p. 32, drought exposure in eastern and south-eastern lowland districts
claims.paraphrase: NDC identifies Nyagatare, Kayonza, Kirehe and Bugesera as dry lowlands with frequent rainfall deficits.
claims.limitations: No district-level impact counts given.

claims.locator: PDF p. 40, crop-yield analysis under wetter and drier RCP8.5 models
claims.paraphrase: The modeled yield functions show crop-specific responses; although wetter conditions often yield net gains, the appendix identifies drier conditions as Rwanda's greatest crop risk.
claims.scenario: RCP8.5 wet (GFDL-ESM2M) and dry (MIROC-ESM-CHEM) climate models
claims.limitations: Modeled, not realized, yields; responses vary by crop.

access_audit.notes: Inspected climate, regional and disaster passages in the full NDC.
Opened the substantive 76-page CCDR technical appendix and inspected climate-scenario methods and crop-yield results.
access_audit.reuse_terms: Noncommercial reproduction with full attribution; additional permissions may apply.

gaps: Opened sources report climate-related disaster losses and mobility but do not establish a country-specific climate-to-violence causal pathway.

sources.title: United Republic of Tanzania Country Climate and Development Report: Executive Summary
sources.temporal_coverage: Current climate-risk exposure and climate-development scenarios through 2050, reported in 2024
sources.methodology: CCDR executive summary reports macroeconomic, climate, sectoral, institutional and financial modeling under climate and growth scenarios.
sources.limitations: Summary-level results are modeled and scenario-dependent; detailed methods are outside this executive summary.

sources.title: Tanzania's Nationally Determined Contribution
sources.organization: United Republic of Tanzania, Vice President's Office (Union and Environment)
sources.temporal_coverage: Observed climate through 2016 and projections through 2090 reported in the 2021 NDC
sources.methodology: NDC draws on the Second National Communication, national adaptation planning and cited Future Climate for Africa projections.
sources.limitations: NDC reports results from earlier studies; its climate-risk assessment methods were still to be developed when submitted.

claims.locator: PDF p. 8, urban flood exposure
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR estimates about 463 km2 of urban area is at high risk of flooding from rivers, rain and sea-level rise; many affected urban residents live in unplanned settlements without adequate drainage.
claims.limitations: Modeled high-risk area is not a count of people or observed flood damage.

claims.locator: PDF p. 8, population exposure to climate risks
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR estimates 27.7 percent of Tanzania's population and 29.4 percent of its vulnerable population are exposed to at least one climate risk.
claims.limitations: The summary aggregates exposure to at least one risk and does not disaggregate by hazard here.

claims.locator: PDF p. 8, agriculture-dependent population vulnerability
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR says about 70 percent of Tanzania's population depends on agriculture, many as poor smallholder farmers, and is poorly positioned to manage repeated or simultaneous climate shocks.
claims.limitations: This is the report's national characterization; the passage does not give a farmer-level impact estimate.

claims.locator: PDF p. 17, observed temperature and drying trends
claims.paraphrase: The NDC reports average maximum temperatures rose over 1 degree C in 1961-2013 and drying occurred in northeastern and much of southern Tanzania during 1981-2016, affecting agriculture, water and energy.
claims.limitations: The NDC summarizes prior national-communication trend analyses through 2016.

claims.locator: PDF p. 18, Future Climate for Africa projections
claims.paraphrase: NDC projects 0.8-1.8 degrees C warming by the 2040s and 1.6-5.0 degrees C by 2090; dry-season rainfall may decline, wet-season rainfall rise, with southern decline and Lake Victoria-area increase by 2030.
claims.scenario: The inspected summary does not specify it.
claims.limitations: Projections cite Future Climate for Africa (2017); rainfall patterns vary by season and region.

claims.locator: PDF p. 17, adaptation targets by 2030
claims.paraphrase: The NDC sets a target to raise access to clean, safe water from 2015 baselines of 86 percent in urban areas and 67.7 percent in rural areas to 100 percent by 2030.
claims.limitations: This is an NDC target; it does not demonstrate achieved 2030 coverage.

access_audit.notes: Inspected exposure and urban-flood passages in the 20-page summary.
access_audit.reuse_terms: Noncommercial reproduction with full attribution; additional permissions may apply.

access_audit.notes: Opened the complete 35-page government NDC and inspected observation, projection and water-target passages.

gaps: The opened Tanzania sources report climate risks and development vulnerabilities but do not establish a country-specific climate-to-conflict or climate-to-violence link.

claims.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 1), recent weather-shock exposure

sources.title: Zambia Country Climate and Development Report: Executive Summary
sources.temporal_coverage: Current impacts and dry-hot scenario projections through 2050, reported in 2026

sources.limitations: Executive-summary results are scenario-specific; detailed methods are outside this document.

sources.title: National Adaptation Plan for Zambia
sources.organization: Government of Zambia, Ministry of Green Economy and Environment
sources.temporal_coverage: Current vulnerability assessment and medium- to long-term adaptation plan, reported in 2023
sources.methodology: NAP uses a qualitative climate-vulnerability and adaptive-capacity matrix.
sources.limitations: Matrix is qualitative, not quantified loss or causal analysis.

claims.locator: PDF p. 7, Key Report Messages
claims.paraphrase: Under the CCDR's BAU dry-hot scenario, drought risk rises fivefold by mid-century and climate change lowers annual GDP about 6 percent by 2050, affecting agriculture, hydropower and labor productivity.
claims.limitations: Scenario-specific model result, not a single expected outcome.

claims.locator: PDF p. 7, Key Report Messages on social protection and disaster risk financing
claims.paraphrase: CCDR says shock-responsive social protection backed by disaster risk financing has cushioned recent drought impacts; it recommends scaling early warning and adaptive social protection.
claims.limitations: Summary does not identify program coverage or isolate causal contribution.

claims.locator: PDF p. 30 (printed p. 23), social vulnerability matrix on drought and water sources
claims.paraphrase: NAP says drought can reduce water quantity and quality; many rural communities rely on a single river or stream, and resulting scarcity affects users across provinces.
affected_groups: rural communities dependent on single water sources
claims.limitations: Qualitative risk matrix; no service-loss or population count.

claims.locator: PDF p. 31 (printed p. 24), groundwater and adaptive-capacity matrix
claims.paraphrase: NAP rates drought-related groundwater exposure high and says low-rainfall areas have lower adaptive capacity because droughts occur frequently, including Southern and Eastern provinces in agro-ecological region I.
claims.limitations: Qualitative area rating; no local trend series is given in this matrix.

claims.locator: PDF p. 34, financial vulnerability matrix for small-scale farmers
claims.paraphrase: NAP links drought yield losses to lower smallholder income from crop, livestock and fish sales, with little adaptation finance in Southern, Western and Eastern provinces.
claims.limitations: Assessment is qualitative and reports no income amount.

claims.locator: PDF p. 30, forestry vulnerability matrix on drought and fire risk
claims.paraphrase: NAP states higher temperatures and drought contribute to more frequent forest-fire risk in Southern, Western, Eastern and Central provinces.
claims.limitations: NAP presents a qualitative risk assessment, not province-level fire incidence counts.
